newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Tortoise takes a breather through its backside.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Tortoise takes a breather through its backside.

text.p: Australian scientists on Tuesday said they were studying a rare freshwater tortoise which breaths through its bottom when underwater and through its mouth when on land.

The Rheodytes Leukops, commonly known as the Fitzroy River tortoise, breathes oxygen through special gills lining its rear passage (cloaca), enabling it to stay under water longer, said zoologist Craig Franklin from the University of Queensland.
"In the six species we have caught, the cloaca appears as a gaping hole about the size of a five-cent (small) coin opening into an abdominal cavity," Franklin said in a statement.
"When the animal is held up to the light, it appears a good part of the abdomen is missing, with gill-like structures hanging inside this large cavity," Franklin said.
Franklin said the unique breathing technique enabled the tortoise to stay underwater for up to five hours, compared with the maximum two hours for other tortoise species.
The Fitzroy River tortoise was first discovered 25 years ago and appears in only four rivers around the coastal town of Rockhampton in Queensland state, one of which is the Fitzroy.
The tortoise, one of only 16 freshwater species in Australia, is classified as vulnerable by wildlife authorities.
